title: Fact-Checkers
sub: How to Know What’s Real · Grades 3–4 · 30 minutes · General / Homeroom
objective: Students will understand that optical illusions demonstrate how easily our eyes and brains can be deceived, and will develop and apply five practical strategies for verifying information before believing or sharing it.
materials: Teacher-created fake social media post example (age-appropriate, obviously fictional)
Chart paper and markers for creating class “Fact-Checker Rules”
**Recommended from Perception Lab:** Checker Shadow (#1), Rotating Snakes (#8), Simultaneous Contrast (#2)
connection: **Option 1 — Visit the Mini Museum:** The exhibition features a 1904 Monarch Stereoscope with original Keystone view cards. Victorian audiences were amazed by these devices just as we’re amazed (and sometimes fooled) by digital manipulation today.
**Option 2 — Virtual Visit:** Explore at minimuseumproject.org/exhibitions/seeing-is-deceiving or view artifacts at minimuseumproject.org/exhibitions/seeing-is-deceiving/artifacts

steps.title: Same or different?
script: **Opening demonstration:** Show the checkerboard shadow illusion (where two squares appear different colors but are identical).

*“I’m going to show you two squares. Tell me: Are they the same color or different colors?”* Take a vote by show of hands. Reveal that they’re identical: *“These squares are EXACTLY the same color! Your brain changed what you saw based on shadows around them.”*

steps.purpose: Take a vote before the reveal, so every student commits to what they see.

steps.title: Is this picture moving?
script: **Second demonstration:** Show a motion illusion (rotating snakes or similar). *“Is this picture moving?”* (It’s completely still, but appears to move.)
*“Your eyes are sending your brain information that isn’t true. This is fun with pictures—but what happens when someone TRIES to trick you on purpose?”*

screen.alt: Circles of blue, yellow and black snake-like rings that seem to turn

steps.purpose: A second trick, then the turn: what if someone tries to trick you on purpose?

steps.title: From optical illusions to real deception
script: *“Optical illusions are fun because we know they’re tricks. But throughout history, people have used visual tricks to fool others on purpose.”*

**Historical example:** Briefly explain spirit photography (1860s–1900s): *“Over 100 years ago, photographers discovered they could make ‘ghosts’ appear in pictures by double-exposing film. They charged grieving families money to ‘photograph’ their dead relatives.”*

**Modern connection:** *“Today, we have ‘deepfakes’—videos made by computers that make it look like someone said or did something they never actually did. And fake pictures and posts spread online every day.”*
*“The good news? Just like you learned the shadow illusion was a trick, you can learn to spot fakes too. Today, you’re becoming Fact-Checkers!”*

steps.purpose: Turn from tricks we enjoy to tricks played on people on purpose, then and now.
students: Optical illusions are fun because we know they’re tricks.

steps.title: Examining a fake post
script: Show your teacher-created fake social media post. Example: A post claiming “Scientists discover chocolate is healthier than vegetables!” with a fake news source.
*“Before I tell you if this is real or fake, what questions should we ask about it?”*
Guide students to generate questions: Who said this? Where did it come from? Does this seem too good to be true?

screen.question: Before I tell you if this is real or fake, what questions should we ask about it?

steps.purpose: Students find the questions a Fact-Checker asks before they are given the rules.
students: Does this seem too good to be true?

steps.title: Our 5 Fact-Checker Rules
script: On chart paper, create the class “Fact-Checker Rules” together. Guide students toward these five strategies:
**STOP before you share:** Take a breath. Don’t pass along information just because it’s exciting or upsetting.
**CHECK the source:** Who created this? Is it from a real, trusted place?
**SEARCH for more:** Can you find this same information from other sources? If only one website says it, be suspicious.
**ASK an adult:** When in doubt, check with a parent, teacher, or librarian before believing or sharing.
**TRUST your gut:** If something seems too amazing, too scary, or too perfect—it might be fake.

steps.purpose: Build the class chart together, one rule at a time.

steps.title: Which rules apply?
script: Give 2–3 quick scenarios and have students identify which Fact-Checker Rule(s) apply:
*“Your friend shows you a video of a celebrity saying something mean. What rules should you use?”* (CHECK the source, SEARCH for more)
*“You see a post saying school is canceled tomorrow, but it’s not from the school website.”* (CHECK the source, ASK an adult)
*“A website says you won a free video game, just click here!”* (TRUST your gut, ASK an adult)

steps.title: Connection to the Mini Museum
script: *“When you visit the Mini Museum, you’ll see real artifacts that tricked people’s eyes over 100 years ago: a stereoscope from 1904 that makes flat pictures look 3D, and illusion cards that transform when you move them. Remember: Understanding HOW tricks work makes you harder to fool!”*
